Article Title: 'We don’t want to leave a white elephant': OCA defends decision to do away with traditional Games village
Article Text:
Containers set up to house athletes from various countries participating in the 20th Asian Games, in Nagoya, Japan. (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NAGOYA: The Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) on Friday defended the Asian Games organisers’ decision to do away with a traditional Games village and accommodate athletes across containers, hotels and cruise ships.The decision to scrap plans for an athletes’ village came after the Games budget more than tripled from the original estimate of 80-100 billion yen (Rs 48.6cr-61cr).OCA director general Husain Al-Musallam said that while an athletes’ village was desirable, its utility after the Games often did not justify the cost of construction.“You spend so much money building the athletes’ village and then we need to see what’s the utilisation of it after the Games. Considering the cost and size of the Games, we need to be a little bit flexible. The athletes’ village is good to look at. But at the end of the day, we need to be practical,” he said at a press conference here on Friday.Tayyab Ikram, head of the OCA coordination commission for the Games, said the decision was driven by the high cost of real estate and the desire to avoid leaving behind a “white elephant” after the Games.“We had clear statistics about what is happening in the real estate values.We don’t want to leave a white elephant after the Games here. It was not easy to discuss, but it was also not a compromise because we found a very unique kind of alternative,” he said.The tradition of an athletes’ village began at the 1982 Asian Games in New Delhi. The hosts of the next two editions — Doha and Riyadh — will have such villages, but Ikram, who is also FIH president, stressed that it was not mandatory for organisers to provide one.TWO-YEAR WAIT FOR BIDIndia’s bid to host the 2038 Asian Games will have to wait until 2028 for a decision on the host nation. India is among six countries to have expressed interest in hosting the Games.“We have received interest from India, Philippines and four other countries to host the Asian Games in 2038. This shows the popularity of the Asian Games,” Al-Musallam said.He said the OCA executive board had already approved the broad evaluation process.“There are 12 more years to go. The calendar is well-established. The executive board has taken a decision to create an evaluation committee to visit all those countries next year and then submit an initial report.“Based on that report, we will have a shortlist and then go for another visit 9-10 years before the Games and submit the final report,” he said.
Article Summary: OCA director general Husain Al-Musallam said that while an athletes’ village was desirable, its utility after the Games often did not justify the cost of construction. India’s bid to host the 2038 Asian Games will have to wait until 2028 for a decision on the host nation.

Article Title: Two Asian Games medals in sight as Quimcy D’Souza, one of the pioneers of teqball in India, leads charge

Manu, Toor to be flagbearers

NAGOYA: Quimcy D’Souza, one of the pioneers of teqball in India, stormed into the semifinals of the sport that is making its Asian Games debut here.Quimcy will face Indonesia’s Sumaya in Saturday’s semifinal, and a win will ensure the first-ever medal for India in teqball, a combination of football and table-tennis played over a curved table.The world No. 24 pulled off a major upset in her Group A women’s singles opener, defeating the top-seed, world No. 7 Yuina Sakamoto of Japan 2-1. After losing the first set 10-12, Quimcy fought back to take the next two 12-11, 13-11 to win in 43 minutes. She followed that up with a 12-9, 12-7 win over Cambodia’s DY Koemyean in just 24 minutes to book her place in the last four.Quimcy had earned a bye in the quarterfinals by virtue of topping her group. If the 24-year-old loses her semifinal to the Indonesian, she will still have a shot at a bronze on Sunday.Quimcy and Mohammed Anas Beg, meanwhile, lost their mixed doubles quarterfinals but won the repechage round 2-0 against Philippines and will now fight for the bronze.The Indian duo lost 0-2 (7-12 10-12) against Vietnam’s Hoang Minh Tan Nguyen and Gia Nghi Trinh in the quarterfinals.Bengaluru-based Quimcy was first drawn to the sport after watching videos of former Brazil football star Ronaldinho playing it.She quit her Mumbai job and moved to B’luru to set up a teqball facility, where she also coaches. “All the four years I have been playing the sport, I’ve only been explaining what it is. But the Asian Games is a huge opportunity for us,” Quimcy told TOI on Thursday.Shooter Manu Bhaker and shot putter Tajinderpal Singh Toor have been named flag bearers of the Indian contingent for Saturday’s opening ceremony. For Toor, it will be another moment of pride after he successfully defended his Asian Games title in Hangzhou. “I’m very proud to be named the flag bearer. It is a moment of great pride for me to be named a flag bearer along with an Olympic medallist (Bhaker),” said Toor

Article Title: 'Maybe 32': Anju Bobby George hopeful of more athletics medals despite Neeraj Chopra miss at Asian Games
Article Text:

(Watch Asian Games live & exclusive on Sony Sports and Sony LIV)

NEW DELHI: The absence of Neeraj Chopra may have taken away Indian athletics’ biggest individual name, but former long jumper Anju Bobby George believes it need not take away from the athletics contingent’s medal ambitions at the Asian Games. The 2003 Paris World Championships bronze medallist expects India’s track and field contingent to cross the 30-medal mark.India won 29 athletics medals — six gold, 14 silver and nine bronze — at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou, its best-ever medal haul in the sport at the continental showpiece. “Neeraj is a big name in athletics, with multiple world-level medals. It is very unfortunate that he is not in our team this time because of an ankle injury. Yes, that’s a setback,” Anju told TOI in an exclusive interview. “But definitely we have many other athletes who are performing well. This time, we are expecting more than last time — more than 30, maybe 32.”For Anju, the defining feature of the current athletics squad is its breadth. Rather than relying on one or two medal contenders, there are podium possibilities across disciplines, particularly the jumps, middle and long-distance events and relays.“This is the beauty of our athletics contingent this time. If you take any event, we are aiming for medals,” she said.The women’s long jump could be one of the most intriguing contests for India in Aichi-Nagoya, with Ancy Sojan and Shaili Singh both entering as serious medal hopes. Ancy, in June this year, jumped 6.88m in Bhubaneswar to break Anju’s 22-year-old national record of 6.83m.“Records are always meant to be broken because that is the path, that’s the growth,” she said. “Otherwise, after I got the World Championships medal, nobody else would’ve done such wonderful achievements for Indian athletics. Ancy is now seasoned, she’s fixed and she’s performing. Shaili is also jumping above 6.80m, but she is yet to set her approach and rhythm and is committing fouls. Otherwise, both jumpers are equally good.We are expecting gold and silver. Either Ancy or Shaili will win gold.”In men’s long jump, Murali Sreeshankar provides another compelling comeback story. The 27-year-old, who missed the Paris Olympics after suffering a patellar tendon rupture in 2024, has returned to top level and produced an 8.38m season-best in June — the second-best jump of his career behind his 8.41m national record.“He is such a tremendous athlete. He was nowhere last year because of the injury. We wonder how he came back, how he conquered again. After injuries, especially in jumps and that too in the take-off leg, coming back is such a big, big thing. He did that with his mental strength,” Anju said.

Article Title: Asian Games 2026: Quimcy Dsouza loses Teqball semifinal, to battle for bronze
Article Text:
Quimcy Dsouza (ANI Photo)

Quimcy loses semifinal after strong start

Indian had topped group with wins over Japan and Cambodia

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Teqball makes Asian Games debut

India’s Quimcy Joaquim Dsouza suffered a 1-2 defeat to Indonesia’s Ima Sumaya in the women’s singles Teqball semifinal at the Asian Games 2026 on Saturday. The 24-year-old will now face Japan’s Yuina Sakamoto in Sunday’s bronze-medal match.A victory in the bronze-medal match would earn India its first-ever Teqball medal at the Asian Games, where the sport is making its debut at the Aichi-Nagoya edition.Making her Asian Games debut, Quimcy began the semi-final on a confident note, taking the opening set 12-7. Sumaya responded in the second set, recovering from an early deficit to edge ahead and level the match with a 12-9 win.Quimcy started the decider strongly, racing to a 3-0 lead before extending it to 4-1. However, Sumaya fought back, took control of the set and closed out the match 12-7 to book her place in the final.The defeat ended Quimcy’s hopes of reaching the gold-medal match, but she will have another opportunity to finish her debut Asian Games campaign on the podium.Quimcy had secured her semi-final berth after topping Group A with two wins, earning direct passage to the last four and avoiding the quarter-finals.She began her campaign with an impressive 2-1 win over top-seeded Japan’s Yuina Sakamoto. After losing the first set 10-12, Quimcy fought back to take the second 12-11 before clinching the decider 13-11.She followed that performance with a straight-sets victory over Cambodia’s Koemyean DY, winning 12-9, 12-7 to finish at the top of her group. Quimcy also competed in the mixed doubles event alongside Mohamed Anas Imran Beg.The Indian pair defeated the Philippines’ Jhoana Abulencia and Prince Agustin in their Group A opener.Teqball, invented in Hungary, combines elements of football and table tennis, using a curved table. The sport resembles a blend of freestyle football and sepak takraw. It is making its Asian Games debut at Aichi-Nagoya 2026, with five medal events: men’s and women’s singles, men’s and women’s doubles, and mixed doubles.Quimcy will now look to cap her debut campaign with a medal when she takes on Sakamoto in Sunday’s bronze-medal match.

Article Title: What makes Asian Games host Nagoya special? A city of cars, football, and sporting legacy
Article Text:
Chunichi Dragons (TOI Photo)

Toshio Kawakita (TOI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NAGOYA: Best known as the home of one of the world’s biggest automobile manufacturers, Nagoya is a blend of industrial might, history and culture. What has largely flown under the radar, however, is the city’s rich sporting tradition, which goes beyond sumo wrestling, kendo or judo.As the Asian Games officially get under way here on Saturday, the Chunichi Dragons, formerly the Nagoya Baseball Club, are celebrating 90 years. Three years after the Dragons were formed, the Nagoya Grampus Eight football club was born.Now known as Nagoya Grampus, the club attracted international attention in the 1990s when it signed England great Gary Lineker and, later, Serbian star Dragan Stojkovic. Lineker spent two seasons in Nagoya before ending his playing career, while Stojkovic enjoyed seven stellar seasons at the club and remains an icon in the city.But the club’s football legacy was shaped just as significantly by a then little-known manager, Arsene Wenger.Wenger spent 18 months at Grampus before heading to Arsenal, where he would go on to become one of the most influential managers of his generation. At a testing stage of his managerial career, the Frenchman embraced the Japanese challenge and transformed Grampus from also-rans into Emperor’s Cup champions in 1995.Under Wenger, the club also won the Japanese Super Cup.For 65-year-old Toshio Kawakita, a lifelong Grampus supporter and now a volunteer at the Asian Games, the combination of Wenger and Stojkovic was the spark that helped reshape football in the city.“Wenger changed the way football was played here. He channelised our players’ passion for the sport and not just taught them tactics, he brought in a sense of purpose and direction. Stojkovic hugely helped Wenger in the process because he arrived here as a player first. Stojkovic returned to our club and under him we won the J League championship in 2010. We owe a lot of who we are as a club to them,” Kawakita said.Another Nagoya old-timer, Iori Tanaka, who runs a ramen shop near the Paloma Mizuho Sports Park, has his own memories of watching Lineker and Stojkovic in action.“Who would have thought that the Europeans would come and play football here? Both were at the fag end of their careers when they came here, but ensured a beginning of something new and lasting,” Tanaka said.Tanaka, though, could not resist a little cricket-related wishful thinking.“Who knows, if your cricketers (from India) play in the Japan Premier League, cricket too will get a huge boost here,” he said with a laugh.As the Asiad brings a generation of international stars to Nagoya, from Olympic champions and world medallists to Asia’s emerging sporting talent, the city is set to become a stage for some of the continent’s biggest names. For a city that has already played host to football greats such as Lineker and Stojkovic, and witnessed Wenger’s transformation of Japanese football, the Games offer a chance to make its sporting heritage part of a bigger story.
Article Summary: The Chunichi Dragons, formerly the Nagoya Baseball Club, are celebrating 90 years. The club attracted international attention in the 1990s when it signed England great Gary Lineker and, later, Serbian star Dragan Stojkovic. Arsene Wenger transformed Grampus from also-rans into Emperor's Cup champions in 1995.

Article Title: ‘A piece of home’: Indian diaspora celebrates women’s team win over Japan in Asian Games opener
Article Text:
Fans celebrate India's win at Japan Asian Games (TOI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NAGOYA: From Tokyo and Osaka to nearby towns such as Yokkaichi, the Indian diaspora drove down to Korogi Athletic Park on the outskirts of the city to watch the ‘pride of India’ in action.The Indian women’s cricket team did not disappoint, making short work of the Japanese challenge for an eight-wicket victory and a place in Sunday’s semifinal against Bangladesh. The result was never really in doubt, but what was striking was the spirit of the hosts and the spunk of the travelling Indian fans.Harmanpreet Kaur-led defending champions, seemingly in no mood for batting practice, opted to bowl first and dismissed Japan for a paltry 57. But not before openers Haruna Iwasaki and Ayaka Kato-Stafford helped themselves to three boundaries between them, drawing loud applause from the home fans and the dugout.The celebratory mood continued when Nonoha Yasumoto and Ayaka Kato-Stafford claimed the wickets of G Kamalini and Bharati Fulmali. For the Indian fans, Shafali Verma provided the entertainment, smashing an unbeaten 40 off just 15 balls, including six boundaries and two sixes.The makeshift stands may have had plenty of empty seats, but the decibel levels generated by the Indian supporters more than made up for it. After all, it is not every day they get to watch their cricketing stars in action on Japanese soil.Japan-born Ishan Kumar Lal, whose parents are from New Delhi, felt the occasion could not have offered a better advertisement for cricket in the country.“Cricket in the Asian Games and India being a part of it is insanely big,” said the towering Japan U-19 all-rounder.Ishan believes matches such as these can provide a much-needed push to the sport’s growing community in Japan.“Watching big teams like these is a great motivation for us to keep doing better and keep advertising cricket in Japan and showing cricket to Japanese people living in Japan and actually make this sport a bigger sport here,” he said.With mini Japan flags fluttering in the stands, it was hard to miss the huge Indian tricolour and placards displaying the fans’ love for their team.Param Vijay Kumar, a Mysuru-born techie living in Osaka, had travelled with a group of friends.“We are grateful that a match has brought a piece of home to us. There was no way we would have missed being here,” he said.For Sukruthi Ajay, originally from Bengaluru, the occasion stirred a strong sense of patriotism.“We are here to support both countries because we love India and we respect Japan. It is a mixed match, but our heart beats for India. To watch our team play in Japan is very special. We are also huge fans of Royal Challengers Bengaluru and it was a delight to watch Smriti Mandhana and Shreyanka Patil as well,” said the homemaker-turned-content creator.
Article Summary: The Indian women’s cricket team made short work of the Japanese challenge for an eight-wicket victory. The result was never really in doubt, but what was striking was the spirit of the hosts and the spunk of the travelling Indian fans. Shafali Verma provided the entertainment, smashing an unbeaten 40 off just 15 balls.

Article Title: ‘Place to rest and get food’: 15 Indian homes on standby as Nagoya chaos hits Asian Games contingent
Article Text:
Nagoya: Japanese Scouts raise the Indian flag during the official welcome and flag-hoisting ceremony for the Indian contingent ahead of the 20th Asian Games, in Nagoya, Japan. (PTI Photo/Arun Sharma)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NAGOYA: With athletes forced to sleep at the registration arena and others enduring endless waits for rooms and buses, the Sports Ministry has stepped in to take stock of the situation facing the Indian contingent here.Sports minister Mansukh Mandaviya , who arrived in Japan on Friday morning, has also sought the support of the 2,000-strong Indian diaspora in Nagoya as efforts intensify to ensure athletes are not inconvenienced.With almost half of the 505-member Indian contingent yet to arrive, a three-layer system has been put in place to streamline their arrival and accommodation.At the airport, two deputy chefs de mission have been deployed to ensure arriving athletes do not have to wait for transport to the athletes’ welcome centre. The ministry has also hired buses so that athletes do not have to depend solely on Games-organiser transport, which has been severely delayed in recent days.At the welcome centre, three Indian officials have been stationed to assist athletes through the registration and accommodation process.With a shortage of hotels in Nagoya and a period of around five days when virtually the entire Indian contingent will be in the city, officials are also anticipating further pressure on accommodation.As a precautionary measure, around 15 homes of Indians living in Nagoya have been kept on standby to provide temporary shelter if required.“Even if they don’t stay there, in case of any delay in allotting accommodation, our athletes will have a place to rest and get some food as well,” a source said.
Article Summary: Sports minister Mansukh Mandaviya has sought the support of the 2,000-strong Indian diaspora in Nagoya. A three-layer system has been put in place to streamline their arrival and accommodation. Two deputy chefs de mission have been deployed to ensure arriving athletes do not have to wait for transport to the athletes’ welcome centre.

Article Title: 'Haar nahi maanunga': Sujeet Kalkal's Asian Games 2026 gold mission on the road to LA Olympics
Article Text:
For Sujeet, the Asian Games is more than just another tournament. It is a fresh start for the wrestler from Haryana’s Bhiwani district.

Three days at Dubai Airport

Father's words gave him strength

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

'Haanikarak baapu'

NEW DELHI: The last time Sujeet Kalkal came close to an Olympic dream, he never even got the chance to step on the mat.Now, as he prepares for his maiden Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, the 23-year-old wrestler is looking at the continental event as the first major marker of a new Olympic journey - one that he hopes will eventually take him to Los Angeles in 2028.“Asaan nahi tha, bhaisaab. Fir se start kiya hai, haar nahi maanunga. Olympics to sapna hai, poora karna hai bass [It wasn’t easy. I’ve started again, and I won’t give up. The Olympics is a dream, and I have to fulfil it, that’s all],” Sujeet told TimesofIndia.com ahead of the Asian Games.There is reason for that confidence. Sujeet enters Aichi-Nagoya having established himself among the leading wrestlers in the 65kg category. He won the Asian Championships in Bishkek earlier this year and has continued to build his credentials in 2026. He also won the 65kg selection trials for the Senior World Championships in Lucknow last week, beating Anuj Kumar 8-3 in the final.The Asian Games, however, will present a different test. Sujeet's 65kg category features some of the biggest names in Asian wrestling, including Japan's Olympic champion Kotaro Kiyooka.Sujeet's competition starts from October 2, when the men's freestyle 65kg, 86kg and 125kg categories will be contested.For Sujeet, the Asian Games is more than just another tournament. It is a fresh start for the wrestler from Imlota village in Haryana’s Bhiwani district.“I was very happy to qualify [for the Asian Games] . It is a fresh start, and I will not disappoint. Behind this success is the hard work of my father, my coach and my entire team. I am in good form. I will come back with the gold medal,” Sujeet said.“The 65kg category is a very challenging and competitive weight category. The world’s best wrestlers always compete in this category. But I have complete faith in my hard work and preparation. My entire focus is only on gold, brother. I have worked very hard,” he added.It will also be a chance to measure how far he has travelled since April 2024, when a three-day ordeal at Dubai International Airport ended his first Olympic campaign before it had even begun.It was April 2024. Sujeet was at Dubai International Airport, waiting to continue his journey to Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, where he was scheduled to compete in the Asian Olympic Qualifying Tournament.But record rainfall had caused floods in Dubai and badly disrupted air travel.Sujeet was stranded at the airport. He could see water everywhere and could only pray that the situation would improve so he could travel to Bishkek, where the qualifiers were scheduled to take place.Sujeet could only watch the time, calculate the days and hours on his fingers, and then sit back. His connecting flight was delayed and eventually remained stranded at the airport for three days.A flight was finally arranged, but by the time he reached Kyrgyzstan and then the venue, it was one and a half hours after the weigh-in had been completed.The Wrestling Federation of India and officials tried their best to find a way to get Sujeet into the competition. But the United World Wrestling rules left them with no option.The opportunity was gone.“I felt very bad. I have no words. It was four years of hard work, and it all ended in that one moment. I was in good form, and everything was over in a moment. I cried alone too, but I had faith in God. I explained things to myself and returned to India,” Sujeet said.Sujeet returned to India devastated. At home, his father Dayanand was waiting for him. Dayanand, a former Greco-Roman wrestler, knew what his son was going through.Sujeet immediately hugged his father. He became emotional and had his father's shoulder to cry on.His father hugged him and told him: “Koi nahi beta, fir se mehnat karenge hum, Olympics khelna hai”.Those words stayed with Sujeet.‘I didn't give up'Starting again was not easy, but Sujeet was adamant. He won gold at the United World Wrestling Ranking Series in Budapest in the men’s 65kg division at the start of 2025. He added two more gold medals to his tally in Zagreb and at the Tirana Grand Prix.He then won a gold medal at the World U23 Championships in 2025 in Novi Sad, Serbia, followed by another gold at the Asian U23 Championships in Vung Tau, Vietnam.He didn't stop there.Sujeet became Asian Champion after winning gold in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. With that gold medal finish, he also rose to the No. 1 ranking in the world.Now, he is set for his first Asian Games. A medal in Aichi-Nagoya would take him another step closer to his next big target - the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.“I didn't give up. I have worked very hard. I have to go a long way. If I had competed in Paris, I would have been 21. I am 23 now. I will be 25 when the Los Angeles Olympics comes around. Age makes a big difference. But I don't want to step back. My mindset is still the same — to win a medal for the country,” he said.For Sujeet, wrestling was never just a sport. His father Dayanand, a former national wrestling champion who also represented India at the World Championships, introduced him to the sport at a very young age. Sujeet was just five when he was pushed into the 'akhaada'.Dayanand could not go to the Olympics to represent India. Now, he wants his son to fulfil that unfulfilled dream.“Papa is very strict," he says."Wo dangal mein haanikarak baapu they na, wo waise hi kuch hain (laughs). He told me, ‘Son, you have to become a wrestler. A wrestler’s son should be a wrestler.’ I have learnt a lot from him since childhood. He is both my guru and my father. Whatever I am today is because of him,” he said.“His dream is to see me at the Olympics and see me win a medal. I will definitely fulfil this dream of my father,” Sujeet signed off.
Article Summary: Sujeet Kalkal is preparing for his maiden Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. The 23-year-old wrestler is looking at the continental event as the first major marker of a new Olympic journey. Sujeet's 65kg category features some of the biggest names in Asian wrestling, including Olympic champion Kotaro Kiyooka.

Article Title: Asian Games: Karate team leaves without coaches; equestrian riders caught in accred maze
Article Text:
Containers set up to house athletes from various countries participating in the 20th Asian Games, in Nagoya, Japan. (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India’s karate team is heading to the Asiad without a dedicated coach while five equestrian riders in Tokyo are scrambling to get accreditation for their personal coaches. Some are even considering a two-hour train journey to Nagoya to sort out the issue in person, TOI has learnt.For the karate contingent, reigning Asian champion Alisha Choudhary’s repeated pleas to sports authorities and Indian Olympic Association (IOA) officials for accreditation for her coach, Vikas Panchal, have gone unheard. The two-member team also includes Chetan Bhatt (men’s kumite 84kg), with Adikessava Peroumal Sinouvassane the designated ‘team leader’.When the sports ministry’s sanction clearing coaches was issued on September 2, no coach was named for karate. Alisha has since sent multiple emails and reminders, underlining that Panchal has trained her for 11 years and guided her to every major international achievement, including her historic gold at the 2026 Asian Karate Championship. He is certified by the World Karate Federation and Asian Karate Federation and has accompanied her to international camps and competitions.Interestingly, during a bout, only a coach can occupy the coaching corner and seek a video review by throwing the challenge block onto the mat. The team leader cannot perform those duties, leaving India’s karate athletes without vital technical and tactical support.The equestrian camp, meanwhile, is caught in its own accreditation scramble. All five foreign coaches are awaiting accreditation and, without it, cannot enter the competition or training venue. The riders are coordinating by phone with IOA contingent staff based in Aichi and Nagoya, a logistical headache made worse by the distance between the two locations.Some riders are now contemplating a roughly two-hour train journey from Tokyo to Nagoya simply to meet IOA officials and get their coaches’ accreditations sorted, potentially losing an entire day of crucial training.It is learnt the five coaches were approved late by the IOA and sports authorities, despite the rider-horse combinations and coaches’ names having been shared with the IOA in May. The riders had also been following up on travel approvals.None of these five coaches are govt funded. Their entire Games expenses will be borne by the riders themselves. Yet, they are still struggling for the accreditation needed to do the job. The accreditation troubles come on top of the equestrian contingent scrambling for hay, bedding and fodder for their horses, with the IOA-appointed ad-hoc committee citing a “shortage of govt funds”.
Article Summary: India's karate team is heading to the Asiad without a dedicated coach. Five equestrian riders in Tokyo are scrambling to get accreditation for their personal coaches. Some are even considering a two-hour train journey to Nagoya to sort out the issue.

Article Title: 'Todos somos caballas': Why Kylian Mbappe is under fire from far-right groups in Spain over a t-shirt
Article Text:
LaLiga - Elche v Real Madrid - Estadio Manuel Martinez Valero, Elche, Spain - September 15, 2026. Real Madrid's Kylian Mbappe rolls up his t-shirt displaying a slogan in solidarity with the people of Ceuta

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Real Madrid forward Kylian Mbappe has come under criticism from conservative and far-right politicians in Spain and France after he did not fully wear a t-shirt supporting residents of Ceuta, Spain's North African territory that is dealing with a migration crisis.Immigration has become one of the biggest political issues in Spain in recent months after a large number of migrants entered Ceuta in July. The debate has also reached football ahead of next year's parliamentary elections.The controversy began before Real Madrid's LaLiga match against Elche on Tuesday. Mbappe, Vinicius Junior and fellow French player Ibrahima Konate partially rolled up t-shirts carrying the message "We are all Ceutans", which was meant to show support for people living in Ceuta, a Spanish territory bordering Morocco.Pictures of the three players quickly spread on social media and drew political reactions.A spokesperson for Spain's opposition Popular Party (PP) said she felt "deep shame" over the incident, while a lawmaker from the far-right Vox party said Spaniards were "perfectly free to feel outraged by three millionaires who live in Spain and then do not support Spaniards".Ultras Sur, a Real Madrid supporters' group linked to the far right and banned from the Santiago Bernabéu, called the players' actions "unacceptable" and demanded public apologies.The incident comes after more than 70,000 migrants crossed into Ceuta from Morocco on July 30 and 31 in a large influx that left scores dead and triggered disagreement within the European Union over immigration.Most migrants returned within hours, but thousands remained in difficult conditions in the city, staying in temporary shelters and makeshift camps. The situation has led to protests by local residents, some of which have been supported by far-right groups.Responding to the criticism, Mbappe said he stood with the people of Ceuta while also remembering migrants who lost their lives."I was in complete solidarity with Ceuta and all the victims.""But I also wanted to make a gesture and express my thoughts for all the immigrants who have lost their lives and who are also living in difficult conditions," he told sports daily AS.Real Madrid also defended its players' right to make their own decision over wearing the t-shirts.Before the match, both Real Madrid and Elche players came out wearing shirts with the slogan "Todos somos caballas" ("We are all mackerels"), with caballas being a nickname for people from Ceuta.Mbappe and Vinicius rolled up their shirts so the message was not visible before removing them as they left the tunnel, while Konate held his shirt in his hands.A Real Madrid official was quoted as saying Reuters that the club agreed to Elche's request to show solidarity with Ceuta but respected different opinions within the squad and allowed each player to decide whether or not to wear the shirt.
Article Summary: Kylian Mbappe comes under criticism for not fully wearing t-shirt supporting residents of Ceuta. Real Madrid players Vinicius Junior and Ibrahima Konate partially rolled up t-shirts carrying the message "We are all Ceutans" The shirts were meant to show support for people living in Ceuta, a Spanish territory bordering Morocco.
